lead: Blood glucose sensors answer one question many times a day: how much glucose is in this drop of blood, or in the fluid under the skin? The disposable strip is the amperometric enzyme electrode made cheap enough to throw away. Continuous monitors turn the same chemistry into a 24-hour trace. People with diabetes use both to dose insulin, catch hypoglycaemia and see how food and exercise move their glucose. This chapter shows how the strip works, what the numbers mean, and where the errors come from.
prereq: You need the amperometric cell from 4.3 and calibration ideas from 4.1.

sections.h3: The strip is a disposable amperometric cell

blocks.text: A glucose strip is a plastic rectangle with a capillary channel. Touch the channel to a blood drop and suction fills it. At the far end sit a working electrode and a reference electrode, printed on the plastic. Dried glucose oxidase (GOx) and a mediator cover the working electrode.

The meter applies a fixed potential and reads current after a few seconds. Current is proportional to glucose. Fill-detection contacts tell the meter the channel is full, so the timer starts only then. This is the amperometric enzyme electrode from 4.3, made disposable.

GOx oxidises glucose to gluconolactone. In early strips oxygen accepted the electrons, and the meter measured either the hydrogen peroxide produced or the oxygen consumed. That made the reading depend on blood oxygen, which changes in illness, at altitude and in poor circulation. A mediator such as ferricyanide (Fe(CN)₆³⁻) or an osmium complex now carries electrons from the enzyme to the electrode. The mediator is oxidised at a lower potential, so fewer substances interfere and the strip reads faster.

sections.h3: Cut-offs, units and the plasma question

blocks.text: Most clinics use these cut-offs: fasting plasma glucose 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or more; 2-hour OGTT 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or more; random glucose 200 mg/dL or more with symptoms; HbA1c 6.5% or more. Hypoglycaemia is below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L). The two units convert as below.

blocks.where: glucose (mg/dL) is the concentration in milligrams per decilitre; glucose (mmol/L) is the same concentration in millimoles per litre.

blocks.text: A meter reads whole blood from a finger. A laboratory usually reports plasma. Plasma glucose is about 11% higher than whole blood, because red cells have less water per unit volume and glucose dissolves in water. Many meters report plasma-equivalent values, but haematocrit still shifts the result: anaemia can read high and polycythaemia can read low. Compare a meter with a lab value only after allowing for this.
HbA1c is not a strip reading. It is a lab measure of average glucose over the past two to three months.

sections.h3: CGM, error sources and the dosing loop

blocks.text: A continuous glucose monitor (CGM) puts a glucose oxidase wire under the skin and measures interstitial fluid. It sends a current every 1–5 minutes. Interstitial glucose lags blood glucose by several minutes, longer when glucose is changing fast. Calibrate with a finger-stick reading when the trace is steady.

Accuracy is reported as MARD, the mean absolute relative difference between sensor and reference readings. Lower is better; many sensors today are below 10%. The trend arrow shows direction and speed, so a reading of 110 mg/dL falling fast is not the same as 110 mg/dL steady.

Error sources: haematocrit; ascorbic acid and uric acid, which oxidise at the electrode and add current; temperature, which changes enzyme rate and diffusion; altitude; expired strips; and reuse. A compression low happens at night when the body presses on the sensor, reducing local blood flow; it reads low without real hypoglycaemia. Confirm with a finger-stick.

The management loop is simple. Self-monitoring gives the number. Correction dose = (current glucose − target glucose) ÷ insulin sensitivity factor (ISF). Meal dose = carbohydrate grams ÷ carbohydrate ratio (CR). A strip costs roughly ₹10–₹50 in India, so cost matters. Reusing a strip or sharing a meter is unsafe: blood-borne infection and strip degradation both follow.

examples.question: A meter reads 212 mg/dL before lunch. The person's insulin sensitivity factor is 1 unit per 50 mg/dL and the target is 120 mg/dL. (a) Convert the reading to mmol/L. (b) Find the correction dose. (c) If 40 g of carbohydrate is eaten and the carbohydrate ratio is 1 unit per 10 g, find the meal dose and the total dose. (d) The reading is 11.8 mmol/L, equal to 212 mg/dL. A user assumes the display is in mg/dL and reads 11.8 as 11.8 mg/dL, a near-hypoglycaemic value, when the true value is about 18 times higher. Using exact conversions, target = 120 ÷ 18 = 6.67 mmol/L and ISF = 50 ÷ 18 = 2.78 mmol/L per unit. Find the correction dose. State what goes wrong if the mg/dL number 212 is fed into a mmol/L sum.
steps: (c) Meal = 40 ÷ 10 = 4.0 units. Total = 4.0 + 1.84 = 5.84 units, given as 5.8 units.

(d) Target = 120 ÷ 18 = 6.67 mmol/L. ISF = 50 ÷ 18 = 2.78 mmol/L per unit. Correction = (11.8 − 6.67) ÷ 2.78 = 1.84 units, about 1.8 units, matching (b). A unit mix-up either cancels the correction dose because 11.8 mg/dL is below any target, or, if 212 is fed into a mmol/L sum, gives a dose many tens of times too large. It is never about 18 times.
examples.answer: The reading is 11.8 mmol/L; correction 1.84 units (1.8), meal 4.0 units, total 5.84 units (5.8). A unit mix-up either cancels the correction dose because 11.8 mg/dL is below any target, or, if 212 is fed into a mmol/L sum, gives a dose many tens of times too large; never about 18 times.
examples.check:
mmol = 212 / 18
corr = (212 - 120) / 50
meal = 40 / 10
total = corr + meal
print(round(mmol, 1))
print(round(corr, 2))
print(round(meal, 1))
print(round(total, 2))
print(round(corr, 1))
print(round(total, 1))

traps: Mixing mg/dL and mmol/L. Divide by 18 to go from mg/dL to mmol/L; multiply to go back.
Comparing a capillary whole-blood meter reading with a laboratory plasma value without allowing for the roughly 11% plasma–whole-blood difference and the haematocrit effect.
Thinking the mediator is the enzyme. Glucose oxidase is the enzyme; ferricyanide or an osmium complex is the electron shuttle.
Treating a CGM reading as blood glucose. Interstitial fluid lags blood, and a compression low can look like hypoglycaemia.
Reusing strips or sharing meters. Both are unsafe and also corrupt the reading.

quiz.q: What does the mediator do in a glucose strip?
quiz.a: It shuttles electrons from reduced glucose oxidase to the electrode, so the meter can measure current without relying on blood oxygen.

quiz.q: Why does a CGM trace lag behind a finger-stick blood glucose reading?
quiz.a: The sensor sits in interstitial fluid; glucose must diffuse from blood to that fluid, so fast changes appear several minutes later.

quiz.q: A fasting plasma glucose is 7.8 mmol/L. Convert to mg/dL and state whether it meets the diabetes fasting cut-off.
quiz.a: 7.8 × 18 = 140.4 mg/dL. It is above 126 mg/dL, so it meets the fasting diabetes cut-off.

quiz.q: A meter reads 250 mg/dL. Target is 100 mg/dL and ISF is 40 mg/dL per unit. Find the correction dose.
A person with anaemia has a meter reading higher than the lab plasma value. Give one reason and the direction of the error.
quiz.a: Low haematocrit changes the blood–plasma water balance and can make the strip read high; the meter overestimates compared with plasma.

quiz.q: At 3 am a CGM shows 62 mg/dL with a flat trend arrow. A finger-stick reads 95 mg/dL. Explain.
quiz.a: This is a compression low: the body is pressing on the sensor, reducing local blood flow. The finger-stick, which measures blood, is more reliable; confirm before treating.

quiz.q: What is MARD and what does a lower value mean?
quiz.a: Mean absolute relative difference between CGM and reference readings; lower means better accuracy.

quiz.q: List three diagnostic cut-offs for diabetes.
quiz.a: Fasting plasma glucose ≥126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L), 2-hour OGTT ≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L), or HbA1c ≥6.5%.

beyond: Not for the exam. Current work pushes CGM toward factory calibration, longer wear and closed-loop insulin delivery. Researchers are testing non-invasive optical and sweat-based glucose sensing, but skin and sweat introduce their own lag and interference. Strip manufacturing is moving to roll-to-roll printing and cheaper mediators. Search for 'continuous glucose monitoring MARD', 'glucose dehydrogenase strip', and 'closed-loop insulin delivery' to go further.
